strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely theoretical question: when and why two-stage RLHF and direct preference optimization (DPO) differ under representation gaps. It provides a useful conceptual taxonomy of model mis-specification regimes and links them to practical empirical observations.

The exact-optimization analysis gives a clear set of conditions under which RLHF, DPO, or online DPO should be preferred, and the high-level intuitions (e.g., reward-model mis-specification favors DPO, policy-model mis-specification favors RLHF, and online DPO can help under isomorphism) are plausible and potentially useful.

The finite-sample separation attempt is interesting: the constructed DTSP task and sparse-recovery arguments aim to formalize a statistical disadvantage of DPO due to learning a value-function-like target rather than a sparse reward. The connection to prior sparse preference-learning work is relevant.

The controlled experiments, though small-scale, provide initial qualitative corroboration of several theoretical claims, and the authors connect their conclusions to existing large-scale empirical studies.
The paper includes a limitations section and does not overclaim beyond its experimental scale.
weaknesses: The central claims about online DPO are not rigorously proved. Propositions 4 and 7 are explicitly justified only by 'numerical proof' (Appendix B.8/B.9), which does not establish the stated existential separation results. Since these propositions support prominent abstract claims ('online DPO cannot bridge the gap' and 'online DPO can outperform both RLHF and standard DPO'), this is a major soundness weakness for a theory paper.

Several theoretical constructions are under-specified or questionable. For example, Proposition 3 uses a feature-symmetry example but does not clearly define the reward model class under which r* is realizable, despite Condition 2 requiring a strong reward model. Other arguments in Appendix B.6/B.7 involve non-compact or constrained policy classes where the DPO argmax may not exist, yet the proofs treat it as attained.

The statistical separation is highly tailored to a specific two-token, duplicated-data construction with strong assumptions on the Gram matrix and feature mapping. It is not clear how generally the claimed DPO inefficiency extends beyond this example, and the lower bound for any DPO estimator is over a specially constructed environment rather than a broad class of realistic policy classes.

The exact-optimization results are mostly straightforward implications of model-class capacity and may not justify the billing as a comprehensive 'dichotomy.' The double-mis-specification analysis in particular relies on specific constructions and numerical illustrations rather than general principles.

The experimental validation is very small-scale (GPT-2-large, 3 seeds) and cannot reliably distinguish the proposed fine-grained regimes. Error bars and statistical significance are not clearly reported, and the code link appears incomplete ('released at' with no URL), hindering reproducibility.

The manuscript is at times difficult to follow: equations are broken or duplicated, notation is inconsistent (e.g., π_OFFO/π_DPO^online confusion), and several appendix sections contain typographical errors. This presentation quality is below the standard expected for a main-track theory submission.

strengths: The paper offers a systematic, well-organized taxonomy of RLHF-vs-DPO performance gaps across mis-specification regimes (Figure 1), which is a genuinely useful conceptual framing for the community.

The finite-sample analysis in Section 4 (Theorems 14/15) is a concrete, rigorously proven separation showing that the DPO surrogate-reward target can be dense even when the true reward is sparse, giving Ω(d/n) versus Õ(k log d/n) for RLHF — an interesting and non-obvious demonstration of a statistical advantage of two-stage learning.
The connections drawn to large-scale empirical studies (Razin et al., Ivison et al., Xu et al., Swamy et al.) are reasonable and help ground the theory.
The limitations section is honest, and reproducibility artifacts (codebase, datasets, hyperparameters, compute) are described in reasonable detail.
weaknesses: The headline novel claims — Propositions 4 and 7, which the abstract highlights as 'online DPO can outperform both RLHF and standard DPO' — are not proven. They are only 'verified numerically' by inspecting gradient curves (Appendices B.8 and B.9). For a theory paper this is a serious evidential weakness: a numerical illustration of a few gradient curves is not a proof of existence, yet it is presented as a proposition.

The exact-optimization results (Propositions 1, 3, 5, 6) are largely straightforward consequences of the definitions and significantly overlap prior work (Swamy et al. 2025 for the isomorphic case; Nika et al. 2024 for related sub-optimality bounds across the same three cases). The marginal originality of Section 3 is therefore limited, and the constructions are simple 3-armed bandits.

The statistical separation (Section 4) is construction-specific. It hinges on an artificial feature mapping ψ(a,b)=ψ(b)+(r_dense^Tψ(a))e_1 and an artificial data-collection scheme (duplicating single-token pairs). The gap is partly produced by the estimator choice: RLHF is handed a sparsity-aware (ℓ0/ℓ1) estimator while DPO is restricted to plain MLE. It is unclear the phenomenon generalizes or that the comparison is fair, so the claim that 'DPO distorts the intrinsic structure of the true reward' is not convincingly established beyond the engineered example.

The double-mis-specification analysis (Conditions 6, 7) concludes that 'either method may win, and it depends on the qualities of the (surrogate) reward models.' This is a weak, somewhat circular conclusion and yields little actionable insight, undercutting the 'understanding' promised by the title.

The empirical validation is small-scale (GPT-2-large on PKU-SafeRLHF) and only qualitative: the 'verifications' match monotone trends rather than testing the predicted rates, and Figure 3 (right) is explained away post hoc by 'the reward model being too weak.' Using a pairwise-regression surrogate instead of PPO and a fixed (not truly ground-truth) reward oracle further weakens the correspondence to the theory.

Presentation/theory gaps: Definition 1 (PILAF sampler) is garbled/broken in the manuscript; Theorem 2 relies on unquantified '∇≈' approximations, and its second-order term is bounded by an expression (δ/(6√3 σ'(R_max+δ))) that can be enormous, so the claimed approximation to the value function is not rigorous. The advertised code URL is also missing.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive theoretical framework that decomposes the RLHF-vs-DPO performance gap into an explicit representation gap under exact optimization and an implicit representation gap under finite samples, yielding a useful taxonomy of when each method is preferred.

The finite-sample separation results (Theorems 10, 11, 14, 15) are a substantial and novel contribution: under a token-level linear parameterization and a sparse-reward construction, RLHF reward learning can exploit sparsity to achieve estimation error O(k log d/n) with l0 or O(sqrt(k log d/n)) with l1, while DPO's surrogate reward estimation is lower bounded by Omega(d/n), leading to a provable sub-optimality separation.

The exact-optimization analysis under different mis-specification conditions (Propositions 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9) offers a clean and mostly rigorous characterization, including constructive counterexamples where either RLHF or DPO can win depending on the relative capacities of the reward and policy model classes.

The token-level analysis of the optimal policy (Equation 1) gives a clear intuition for why DPO's learning target is more complex than the reward model's: the policy must capture a recursively defined q* function that entangles the reward with the reference policy, which helps explain sample inefficiency and mis-specification vulnerability.

The paper connects its theoretical predictions to several existing large-scale empirical studies and provides controlled small-scale experiments that qualitatively corroborate the predicted trends, making the theory more grounded.
The authors include an explicit limitations section and provide implementation details, which aids reproducibility (though the code URL appears missing in the manuscript).
weaknesses: Two headline propositions (Proposition 4 and Proposition 7) are only verified numerically rather than rigorously proven, despite being central to the claimed dichotomy (e.g., online DPO cannot close the gap under policy mis-specification; online DPO can outperform both RLHF and standard DPO under isomorphic mis-specification). In a theory paper, numerical gradient curves are not a substitute for a formal proof of existence, which weakens the completeness of the main claims.

The finite-sample separation relies on a highly specific and artificial task (dual-token sparse prediction) with linear token-level parameterization, known sparsity structure, a constrained estimator, and a specially designed feature mapping. It is unclear how far this separation generalizes to practical neural reward/policy models, and the paper itself acknowledges the parameterization and estimators are tailored to the task.

The exact-optimization results, while useful as a taxonomy, are largely intuitive and follow from basic realizability/mis-specification arguments; several proofs are simple inequalities or small bandit constructions. The novelty in this part is moderate compared to prior work such as Swamy et al. (2025) and Nika et al. (2024).

The experimental verification is small-scale (GPT-2-large, 5k-10k samples, 3 seeds) and uses proxies such as pairwise regression instead of PPO and layer freezing to simulate mis-specification. The plots lack visible error bars/variance, and it is not clear that the experimental conditions faithfully instantiate the theoretical conditions.

The paper has presentation issues: some notation inconsistencies (e.g., V_{r^\star}^{\eta} in the introduction), broken equations in the extracted text, a missing code URL, and a somewhat tangential 'Bonus' appendix section that is not fully integrated into the main narrative.

Theorem 2 is an approximate result with unspecified Lagrangian remainders and relies on the PILAF sampler; its practical implications depend on the second-order deviation being small, which may not hold when the reward scale is large or the reward model is poorly fitted. The theorem is more heuristic than exact.
The paper does not include an explicit ethics statement, though the topic raises no obvious ethical concerns.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important theoretical question—when and why two-stage RLHF and DPO differ—and provides a reasonably comprehensive case analysis (Table 1: no mis-specification, policy-only, reward-only, and double mis-specification), which extends prior work such as Nika et al. (2024) and the isomorphic case of Swamy et al. (2026).

The statistical separation results (Theorems 10/11 and their formal versions 14/15) are a genuine and useful advance: by constructing the Dual-Token Sparse Prediction task they show reward learning can leverage sparsity (Õ(k log d/n) with ℓ0, Õ(√(k log d/n)) with ℓ1) while any DPO estimator is lower bounded by Ω(d/n), even without mis-specification. This cleanly formalizes the intuition that DPO's need to fit the (dense) soft value function q* distorts the intrinsic structure of the reward.

The paper connects its theory to several independent large-scale empirical studies (Section 5.2: Razin et al., Swamy et al., Xu et al., Ivison et al.), which strengthens the practical plausibility of the qualitative claims beyond the authors' own small-scale experiments.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: public datasets (PKU-SafeRLHF variants), public base/reward models (GPT-2-Large, GPT2-large-harmless), named open-source codebases, and detailed hyper-parameter/compute descriptions; a limitations section is included.
The gradient/objective analysis in Appendix B and the general 'π_RLHF = argmax V_{r_RLHF}, π_DPO = argmax V_{r_DPO}' principle (Eq. 2) give a coherent unifying lens for interpreting the comparisons.
weaknesses: The exact-optimization 'dichotomy' (Propositions 3–9) is established almost entirely via small three-armed bandit constructions with hand-picked feature maps (e.g., ψ(a3)=½ψ(a1)+½ψ(a2)). These are valid existence proofs, but the paper itself concedes 'relatively simple techniques,' and the results are sensitive to the specific constructions, limiting how much they reveal about realistic language-model settings.

The central sample-complexity separation rests on a highly engineered construction (DTSP, Assumptions 12–13): ψ(a,b)=ψ(b)+(r_dense^T ψ(a))e1, duplicated first/second tokens (a1a1, a2a2), known second-token parameter θ1=e1, and a deliberately dense value-function component. The whole gap hinges on r_dense being dense; the claim that the intuition generalizes is argued informally (Section 4 'concluding remarks') rather than proven, so the separation is narrower than the abstract suggests.

The empirical validation of Section 3 uses a pairwise-regression surrogate instead of PPO, and for 'exact optimization' regresses the policy's implicit reward against the ground-truth reward oracle. This is not standard two-stage RLHF, so the experiments test a proxy of the method rather than the method itself, weakening the connection between the experiments and the theoretical claim being 'confirmed.'

Experiments are small-scale (GPT-2-Large-774M, PKU-SafeRLHF, 1k–9k samples, 3 seeds) and the authors admit the diffs are often small; several figure-to-theory attributions (e.g., Figure 2 right) are asserted rather than quantitatively verified, so the empirical corroboration is suggestive, not decisive.

Presentation quality is uneven and hinders verification: Table 1 is garbled in the provided version ('VπRLHF = VπDPO + VπDPO + …'), there is a truncated sentence ('Our codes are released a'), several typos ('Lagangian', 'exisiting', 'fundational', 'behavior' vs 'behaviour'), notation inconsistencies (π_θ(x,y|x), r_θ(x,y) vs r_θ(y), Vπ4/Vπ6), and duplicate/mislabeled references (two 'Feng et al. 2024', inconsistent Razin et al. years).

Theorem 2 largely reproduces the objective-level analogue of Feng et al. (2025) from a gradient to an objective perspective, so parts of the exact-optimization analysis offer limited additional insight beyond existing PILAF/online-DPO theory, and the denominator/bound details (e.g., the ε bounds) are hard to check from the main text alone.

strengths: The paper provides a unified framework that categorizes the RLHF-vs-DPO gap into four misspecification regimes (strong/weak reward x strong/weak policy) plus a finite-sample regime, which is pedagogically useful for organizing the scattered literature.

The separation result (Theorem 10/11) is the most interesting contribution: it shows that even when the reward and policy classes have the same dimension (d_R = d_P = d) and under realizability, an intrinsic sparsity in the reward (k << d) can induce a genuine sample-complexity gap because the DPO target (q*/v* function) entangles the reward with the base model and becomes dense. This is a concrete mechanism rather than a mere scaling-in-dimension argument.

The authors connect their theoretical predictions to several existing large-scale empirical studies (Xu et al. 2024b; Ivison et al. 2024; Rafailov et al. 2023; Razin et al. 2026; Swamy et al. 2026), which helps ground the abstract results.
The limitations section is honest: the authors acknowledge they offer no theoretically-grounded alternative to the BT-based reward learning they critique, and that their experiments are small-scale.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Proposition 1 (full realizability => both attain V^Pi) follows immediately from the definitions and is explicitly acknowledged as a well-known baseline; Theorem 2 is stated by the authors themselves to be 'analogous to Theorem 4.1 in Feng et al. (2025)'; Proposition 6 (isomorphism => equality) is directly attributable to Swamy et al. (2026). The main separation theorems (10, 11) are essentially translations of Yao et al. (2025) (sparse-recovery rates) and Zhu et al. (2023) (MLE and lower-bound rates) to a bespoke DPO setting. Much of Section 3 reduces to the observation that argmax over a larger class is at least as good, i.e., 'if the reward class is misspecified but the policy class is realizable, direct policy optimization wins, and vice versa.'

Several propositions are near-trivial and their strict-gap witnesses are strawmen. Propositions 3 and 5 show RLHF ≥ DPO (resp. DPO ≥ RLHF) using simple 3-armed bandit constructions with a feature map psi(a_3) = 0.5 psi(a_1) + 0.5 psi(a_2). The constructions demonstrate no more than the definitions already imply and do not establish that these regimes are the practically relevant ones.

The DTSP construction underlying Theorem 10/11 is heavily engineered. Assumption 12 imposes psi(a,b) = psi(b) + (r_dense^T psi(a)) e_1, and Assumption 13 requires duplicating the first token into a second token. The separation depends on the reward model being given an ℓ0-constrained oracle (knowledge that ||theta_0||_0 <= k) while the DPO estimator is plain MLE — an apples-to-oranges comparison. The claim that this reflects general practice ('DPO distorts the intrinsic structure of the true reward') is asserted rather than demonstrated; whether real reward sparsity survives the q*-recursion is not addressed empirically.

The experimental corroboration is weak relative to the theory. The core quantitative predictions (e.g., O(k log d/n) vs O(d/n), the Ω(d/n) lower bound, the sqrt-d factors in Theorem 11) are never measured; the experiments only check qualitative ordering of scores on GPT-2-Large / PKU-SafeRLHF. The mapping from the abstract Conditions 1-4 to the concrete modifications (freezing half the blocks, swapping to a linear head, scaling r_margin) is heuristic, and the 'verification' of Theorem 2 via three reward scales (Fig. 1) is too coarse to distinguish the second-order deviation term from confounders.

Presentation issues: Table 1 is rendered as garbled repeated tokens ('VπRLHF = VπDPO + VπDPO + ...'), which obscures a headline summary; the online-DPO loss equations involve confusing/likely erroneous sg() usage; several formulas in the appendix are mangled (e.g., σ''(R_max + δ) missing arguments, inconsistent θ_p,t ψ(y_{0..t}) vs ψ(y_{0..t-1},s)); and the code-release statement is truncated ('Our codes are released a').

Framing overstates the practical takeaway. The abstract and Section 4 conclude that 'the reward model's quality typically surpasses that of the DPO model' and thereby explain empirical RLHF advantages, but this rests on the sparsity assumption and on F ⊆ F_Pi; the paper's own Proposition 9 shows the opposite ordering in a larger-reward-class regime, so the 'typical' conclusion is not supported by the theory as stated.

strengths: Provides a comprehensive theoretical taxonomy of RLHF vs. DPO performance across exact optimization and finite-sample regimes, explicitly removing the common realizability assumption and covering reward-only, policy-only, double, and isomorphic misspecification cases.

The results yield useful and nuanced insights, especially that online DPO can outperform both RLHF and standard DPO under isomorphic model classes, while under policy misspecification online DPO cannot close the gap to RLHF.

The finite-sample separation in the dual-token sparse prediction task is a meaningful theoretical contribution: it gives a concrete construction where reward learning can exploit sparsity while DPO’s surrogate reward must learn a denser value-function-like target, leading to provable statistical inefficiency for DPO.
The controlled experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF with GPT-2-Large qualitatively corroborate the theoretical predictions across several misspecification conditions and sample-size regimes.
The paper connects its findings to several recent large-scale empirical studies, which strengthens the practical relevance of the theoretical claims.
Limitations are acknowledged honestly, and no material ethical concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Several exact-optimization propositions follow fairly directly from the definitions and standard performance-difference arguments; while the taxonomy is useful, the technical novelty of these parts is moderate.

The main finite-sample separation relies on a highly specific DTSP construction, including a carefully designed feature map, duplicated-token data collection, known dense component/offset structure, and strong sparsity/well-conditioned Gram matrix assumptions. This makes the separation convincing as a constructed example but limits how directly it generalizes to practical RLHF/DPO settings.

The comparison between RLHF and DPO in the separation theorem is not entirely apples-to-apples: RLHF is allowed to use a sparsity-aware estimator, while the DPO estimator is an unconstrained dense MLE over the surrogate reward. The paper argues this is intrinsic to DPO, but the practical reach of the conclusion depends on the model parameterization and whether structured policy models could partially recover sparsity.

Experimental validation is limited to small-scale GPT-2-Large models and a single dataset family. The empirical results support the qualitative theory, but they do not provide strong evidence about larger-scale modern LLM training regimes.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: hyperparameters and datasets are described, but the code link appears incomplete/truncated in the appendix, and some implementation details would be difficult to reproduce exactly from the text alone.

The presentation has some typos and formatting issues (e.g., the surrogate reward definition in the preliminaries, inconsistent notation, and repeated/garbled table entries in the extracted manuscript), which reduce clarity.
